title: Ignatius to the Ephesians
subtitle: a prisoner on the road to the beasts writes of one bread, one overseer and the God who came in the flesh
lead: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, was being taken under guard to Rome to die by the wild beasts. At Smyrna, on the coast of Asia, the church of Ephesus sent its overseer Onesimus, the deacon Burrhus and three others to meet him (1:3-2:1). He wrote this letter to thank them. It is the longest of his seven letters, and it carries all his great themes: the church is one, gathered around its overseer, its council of elders and its deacons, like a choir singing one song (3-6); Christ is truly God and truly human, 'God in man', against teachers who said he only seemed to suffer (7; 18-19); and the church's one bread is 'the medicine of immortality' (20:2).

The letter is full of pictures: the cross as a building crane that lifts the stones of God's temple (9:1), believers as 'God-bearers' in procession (9:2), a star that outshone the sun and moon (19:2). It shows how Christians a generation after the apostles echoed Paul, in language that sometimes comes close to John's, and it is quoted to this day in arguments over bishops and over the Lord's Supper. No church counts it as Scripture. It is in no Bible, though Ignatius is honored as a martyr by the Catholic and Orthodox churches, the Episcopal Church, and a district calendar of the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod.
facts: No church. It is not among the New Testament books listed by the Council of Trent (Catholic), Article VI of the Church of England, the Westminster Confession (Reformed), the Second London Baptist Confession, or the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's list of 35 New Testament books. Eusebius's list of accepted, disputed and rejected books (Church History 3.25) does not mention it at all; he treats Ignatius's letters as the writings of a church leader (3.36; 3.38.1).

Ignatius of Antioch, also called Theophorus (1:0). Eusebius calls him bishop of Antioch, 'second in succession to Peter' (Church History 3.36.2); Jerome 'third bishop of the church of Antioch after Peter' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16).

Early in the second century, on the journey to Rome. Eusebius's Chronicle puts the martyrdom 'in the tenth year of Trajan, i.e. 108 A.D.' (Lake); Jerome says he 'was put to death the eleventh year of Trajan'. Lake: modern critics are 'by no means unanimous', but there is 'a general tendency to think that Ignatius was really a martyr in Rome in the time of Trajan (98-117 A.D.)'.
Written at Smyrna (modern Izmir, Turkey), where Ignatius was held and where Polycarp was overseer (21:1), to Ephesus, down the coast to the south.
A letter of thanks and counsel, with a creed-like passage on Christ (18:2-19:3).

The short (Lightfoot's 'middle') recension, as Kirsopp Lake prints it (Loeb, 1912). Lake's witnesses: the Greek Codex Mediceus Laurentianus at Florence (G), the interpolated long recension (g), Grosseteste's Latin (L, about 1250), the Armenian (A, from a lost Syriac), and the Syriac (S). Lake: the text 'may be regarded as fairly accurate, though it is probably by no means so good as that of I. Clement'.
authorship: The witness of the early church

Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, Ignatius's host, sent copies of 'the letters of Ignatius' to Philippi soon after (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2) and names 'the blessed Ignatius' among the martyrs (Polycarp to the Philippians 9:1). Irenaeus, about AD 180, quotes Ignatius to the Romans 4:1 as the words of 'a certain man of ours ... condemned to the wild beasts' (Against Heresies 5.28.4). Eusebius names the seven letters and says Ignatius wrote to Ephesus from Smyrna, mentioning 'Onesimus, its pastor' (Church History 3.36.5); Jerome lists the same seven (Lives of Illustrious Men 16).

Lake explains that the letters survive in three forms: a 'long recension' of thirteen letters, in which the seven are 'greatly corrupted by obvious interpolations'; the 'short recension' of the seven, restored by Ussher from Grosseteste's Latin (1644) and printed in Greek by Vossius (1646); and a Syriac abridgment of three letters found by Cureton (1845). The Catholic Encyclopedia dates the long recension to 'the latter part of the fourth century' and thinks it the work of 'an Apollinarist of Syria or Egypt'.

Before 1644 only the long form was known, and its genuineness 'was often doubted' (Lake). Calvin wrote that 'Nothing can be more nauseating, than the absurdities which have been published under the name of Ignatius' (Institutes 1.13.29). The Catholic Encyclopedia reports that the reformer Dallaeus (1666) questioned all seven letters, that the Anglican Pearson answered him (1672), and that Cureton (1846) held only his three Syriac letters genuine, until Lightfoot 'and others showed it to be merely an abridgment' (Lake). Lightfoot judged that the short Greek 'can hardly have been made later than the middle of the second century' (The Christian Ministry, page 49). In 1910 the Catholic Encyclopedia wrote: 'While it can hardly be said that there is at present any unanimous agreement on the subject, the best modern criticism favors the authenticity of the seven letters mentioned by Eusebius', naming Zahn, Lightfoot and Harnack. Later in the twentieth century the question was opened again. Sergio Zañartu's survey of the recent discussion (Teología y Vida, 2009) names R. Weijenborg (1969), who argued that the short recension was made from the long one; R. Joly (1979), who held the letters a forgery written in Smyrna between 165 and 168; J. Rius-Camps (1980), who kept as genuine only the four letters written from Smyrna; R. M. Hübner (1997), who dated the letters between 165 and 175; and his student T. Lechner (1999). Zañartu quotes W. R. Schoedel (1987), who expected the short recension to remain what 'the scholarly consensus today' sees in it, 'a collection of genuine letters of Bishop Ignatius of Antioch', and C. Munier's survey of a century of research (1993), which found no reason in 'the general opinion of historians and patrologists' to give up the conclusions of the nineteenth-century scholars. Zañartu himself, after weighing the objections, holds to the short recension's authenticity 'until the contrary is proved' (the quotations from his survey are the site's translations). On the other side, B. A. Zuiddam (Ekklesiastikos Pharos, 2010) argues that the seven-letter text may be a medieval abridgment, and that either the whole collection is 'a pious fraud to strengthen orthodoxy of a later date' or eleven letters are Ignatius's own.

audience.to: The church of Ephesus, the chief city of the Roman province of Asia: an old church founded in Paul's time, with an overseer, Onesimus, a council of elders and deacons, which had just sent Onesimus, the deacon Burrhus, Crocus, Euplus and Fronto to Smyrna to meet Ignatius (1:3-2:1). Traveling teachers with 'evil teaching' had passed through, and the church had turned them away (9:1).
audience.why: Lake gives four aims: to thank the church for its kindness (the 'immediate purpose'), 'to strengthen respect for the bishop and presbyters', to protest 'against the form of heresy called docetism', which held that Christ's sufferings were 'merely an appearance', and to secure help for the church in Antioch. Knowing the audience changes the tone: Ignatius is not correcting a church in disorder; he praises a healthy church (6:2; 8:1; 9:1) and urges it to stay one, to meet often (13:1), and to hold to a Christ who truly came in the flesh.
views: Some verses suggest real tensions: some stayed away from the common gathering (5:3, where Lake notes Ignatius may be 'referring to some special instance'), and the overseer's silence was held against him (6:1).
Ignatius repeatedly says the Ephesians already do what he asks (4:1; 6:2; 8:1; 9:1), and Lake names thanks as the letter's first purpose.

outline: Thanks for Onesimus, Burrhus, Crocus, Euplus and Fronto
One mind with God and the overseer; the choir
The false teachers; the one doctor; the stones raised by the cross
Pray for outsiders; answer evil with good
The last times; Paul and the Ephesians
Meet more often; faith and love
Those who ruin the faith; the ointment and the ruler of this age
The cross; Christ conceived, born and baptized; the three mysteries and the star
The second little book; the one bread
Farewell and the church in Syria

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a historical source: Ignatius and his journey as Eusebius and Lake tell it, the three recensions and why the short one is accepted, the Ephesian church and its overseer Onesimus, and the date.

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Follows the New Testament in the letter: Paul's Ephesians and 1 Corinthians, language close to John's ('God's bread', where Lake's margin gives John 6), Matthew's star and anointing, the one formula quotation of Proverbs 3:34 in the form of James and 1 Peter, and what Ignatius knew of Paul's letters.

lenses.name: Church order and the churches
lenses.desc: Reads the letter for the church it shows (one overseer, a council of elders, deacons; the thanksgiving and the one bread) and for how today's churches read it, each from a source that discusses Ignatius.

sections.b: All that is known of Ignatius comes from his letters and from Eusebius, who says that he 'was sent from Syria to Rome, and became food for wild beasts on account of his testimony to Christ', and that on the way, under 'the strictest military surveillance', he strengthened the churches by word and letter (Church History 3.36.3-4). From Smyrna he wrote to Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles and Rome; from Troas to Philadelphia, Smyrna and Polycarp (3.36.5-10). He calls his guards 'ten leopards' (Ignatius to the Romans 5:1). In this letter he is 'on my way from Syria in chains' (1:2), hoping to die well and so to be 'a disciple'.

sections.h: The seven letters and the three recensions
sections.b:
For centuries Ignatius was read in a long, interpolated form with extra letters. In 1644 Archbishop Ussher restored the short form of the seven letters from a medieval Latin version, and in 1646 Isaac Vossius printed the Greek from a manuscript at Florence, which lacks Romans; Ruinart printed Romans from a Paris manuscript in 1689 (Lake). The Syriac abridgment Cureton found in 1845 was at first thought the original, but Lightfoot and others showed it to be an abridgment. The site translates the short recension.

In 1910 the Catholic Encyclopedia wrote: 'While it can hardly be said that there is at present any unanimous agreement on the subject, the best modern criticism favors the authenticity of the seven letters mentioned by Eusebius', naming Zahn, Lightfoot and Harnack. Later in the twentieth century the question was opened again. Sergio Zañartu's survey of the recent discussion (Teología y Vida, 2009) names R. Weijenborg (1969), who argued that the short recension was made from the long one; R. Joly (1979), who held the letters a forgery written in Smyrna between 165 and 168; J. Rius-Camps (1980), who kept as genuine only the four letters written from Smyrna; R. M. Hübner (1997), who dated the letters between 165 and 175; and his student T. Lechner (1999). Zañartu quotes W. R. Schoedel (1987), who expected the short recension to remain what 'the scholarly consensus today' sees in it, 'a collection of genuine letters of Bishop Ignatius of Antioch', and C. Munier's survey of a century of research (1993), which found no reason in 'the general opinion of historians and patrologists' to give up the conclusions of the nineteenth-century scholars. Zañartu himself, after weighing the objections, holds to the short recension's authenticity 'until the contrary is proved' (the quotations from his survey are the site's translations). On the other side, B. A. Zuiddam (Ekklesiastikos Pharos, 2010) argues that the seven-letter text may be a medieval abridgment, and that either the whole collection is 'a pious fraud to strengthen orthodoxy of a later date' or eleven letters are Ignatius's own.

Ephesus was where Paul had lived for more than two years (Acts 19:10), whose elders he called to Miletus (Acts 20:17), and to which the first letter of Revelation is addressed (Revelation 2:1-7). By Ignatius's time it has a single overseer, Onesimus, 'a man of love beyond words' (1:3). Whether he is the slave Onesimus of Paul's letter to Philemon is discussed on the topic page Onesimus; Lightfoot says of the overseer, 'nothing more is known' (The Christian Ministry, page 49).

sections.h: The overseer, the elders and the deacons
sections.b: No early writing presses unity with the overseer harder. The council of elders is tuned to him 'as strings are to a lyre' (4:1); whoever is not 'within the altar' goes without God's bread (5:2); 'we ought to look at the overseer as at the Lord himself' (6:1). Lightfoot wrote that 'no more uncompromising advocacy of the episcopate can be found' and that Ignatius 'values the episcopate chiefly as a security for good discipline and harmonious working in the Church' (The Christian Ministry, pages 84-85). How the churches read this, as the order the apostles left, or, with Lightfoot, as a development out of the council of elders that the last apostles sanctioned, is set out on chapter 5's page, with links to the cards at Acts 20:28, 1 Timothy 3, Philippians 1:1, Titus 1 and 2 Timothy 2:2.

sections.h: The thanksgiving and the one bread
sections.b: Ignatius urges the Ephesians to 'come together more often for the thanksgiving to God' (13:1), and he ends with 'breaking one bread, which is the medicine of immortality, the antidote against dying' (20:2). The Plain English Translation says 'the thanksgiving' for the Greek eucharistia, as it does in the Didache, so the reader sees one Greek word across the early writings and the site does not choose between 'Eucharist', 'Lord's Supper' and 'Communion'. The note at 20:2 gives how the churches read the phrase.

sections.h: Christ in the flesh, against those who deny it
sections.b: Some teachers of Ignatius's day said Christ only seemed to have a body and only seemed to suffer (Lake: 'docetism', from Greek dokein, 'to seem'). Ignatius's answer runs through the letter: Christ is 'God in man', 'first able to suffer and then beyond suffering' (7:2); he 'was carried in the womb by Mary', born and baptized (18:2); at his coming 'God was made known in a human way' (19:3). The topic pages The Incarnation and Docetism follow the thread through the Bible.

Ignatius quotes with a formula only once: 'For it is written, "God takes his stand against the proud"' (5:3), Proverbs 3:34 in the form James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 use. Everything else is echo: Paul's Ephesians in the greeting, 1 Corinthians in chapters 15-18 (Lake's margin), 'God's bread', in the words of John 6:33 (5:2), Matthew's star and anointing (17:1; 19:2). The notes give each in the site's own wording where Ignatius's Greek matches, and in his own words where it does not.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a letter built around silence
spec.body: Silence appears at three turning points: the overseer 'keeping silent' (6:1), Christ who did things 'in silence' and whose 'quiet' can be heard (15:1-2), and the mysteries 'done in God's quiet' (19:1). Read together, they suggest that Ignatius is defending a quiet overseer against fluent visiting teachers by showing that God's own greatest works were silent. This is Claude's reading of the letter's structure; it has not been checked against published scholarship.

spec.title: Claude's observation: the 'one doctor' and the 'medicine' frame the teaching
spec.body: The doctor appears in 7:2, right after the 'bite' of false teaching that is 'hard to heal', and his medicine appears in 20:2, at the end of the teaching. Between them lies the whole account of Christ's coming. The letter's doctrine is framed as a cure: Christ heals by being truly human and truly God, and the church takes his medicine at the one table.

canon.summary: An early Christian letter from about the reign of Trajan (98-117), by Ignatius of Antioch on his way to martyrdom in Rome. No church counts it as Scripture: it is in no Bible. Catholic and Orthodox churches, the Episcopal Church and a district of the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod honor Ignatius as a martyr, and his letters are read as a witness to the faith of the generation after the apostles.
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books (1546) does not include it. The U.S. bishops keep 17 October as the 'Memorial of Saint Ignatius of Antioch, Bishop and Martyr', and the Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes 20:2 on the Eucharist (paragraph 1405).

The Orthodox Church in America commemorates 'Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bishop of Antioch' on 20 December; its life of him names the seven epistles and Irenaeus's quotation of the letter to Rome. It is not read as Scripture.
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books, the 27 and eight more (among them 'The book of Clement' and the 'Didascalia'), does not name it.

Not Scripture: the Thirty-Nine Articles (Article VI) receive 'All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'. The Episcopal Church's trial calendar Holy Women, Holy Men commemorates 'Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, and Martyr, c. 115' on 17 October and calls his 'Seven authentic letters' valuable for the life of the early church.

The calendar of the church's Southern District commemorates 'Ignatius of Antioch, Pastor and Martyr' on 17 October, and says his letters stressed 'the full humanity and deity of Christ, the reality of Christ's bodily presence in the Lord's Supper, the supreme authority of the bishop, and the unity of the Church'. That is a district page; the synod's own calendar was not opened.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament as 'all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these'.
Not Scripture: the Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 New Testament books, 'All of which are given by the inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life'.

provenance.h: Written at Smyrna on the road to Rome
provenance.b: Ignatius wrote from Smyrna, where he was held with Polycarp's church (21:1), to the church at Ephesus, which had sent five men to him (1:3-2:1). Eusebius, writing about AD 325, places it first among the letters from Smyrna (Church History 3.36.5), and Lake follows that order.

Soon after, the Philippians asked Polycarp for Ignatius's letters, and he answered: 'As you asked, we have sent you the letters of Ignatius, the ones he sent us, and the others we had here with us' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2). Eusebius quotes the passage (Church History 3.36.15).

The Greek of the short form survives in one manuscript, the Codex Mediceus Laurentianus at Florence (G), published by Vossius in 1646. Lake checks it against the interpolated long recension (g), the Latin version made about 1250 by Robert Grosseteste of Lincoln from a lost Greek copy (L), the Armenian, made from a lost Syriac (A), and Syriac fragments (S). Lake's footnotes mark sixteen places in this letter where witnesses or editors differ; the site's variants give them.

rejected_why.h: Written after the apostles, by one who claims no apostle's authority
rejected_why.b: Ignatius writes as a disciple, not an apostle: 'I do not command you as though I were someone ... I have only made a start at being a disciple' (3:1), and in his letter to Rome he says he does not command 'as Peter and Paul' did, for 'they were apostles' (Ignatius to the Romans 4:3). The early church gathered as its New Testament the writings it held to come from the apostles and their circle, and Ignatius stood outside that circle by his own account.

Eusebius's survey of the accepted, disputed and rejected writings names the Shepherd and the Epistle of Barnabas among the rejected (Church History 3.25.4) but does not name Ignatius's letters at all; he presents them among the works of those who 'transmitted the apostolic doctrine to us in writings' (3.37.4-3.38.1), that is, as the letters of a church leader.

rejected_why.h: A corrupted text in the Middle Ages
rejected_why.b: For centuries the letters circulated in the long, interpolated form with forged additions, and their genuineness 'was often doubted' (Lake). That history made some Protestant readers distrust anything under Ignatius's name, Calvin among them (Institutes 1.13.29). It bears on how the letters are judged as history, not on any claim to be Scripture, which they never made.

cited_in.b: Paul's farewell to the elders of Ephesus on his way to Jerusalem. Ignatius, on the same kind of road, calls the Ephesians 'fellow initiates' of Paul and the road the martyrs take (12:2). Acts 20 calls the same men both 'elders' (20:17) and 'overseers' (20:28), where Ignatius has one overseer over a council of elders.

The risen Christ praises the church at Ephesus for testing false apostles and not tolerating evil people (Revelation 2:2). Ignatius praises the same church for stopping its ears to traveling teachers (9:1).

Paul's Onesimus and Ignatius's 'Onesimus, ... your overseer' share a common slave name; whether they are one man is argued on the topic page Onesimus. Lightfoot says of the overseer, 'nothing more is known'.
Paul 'fought with wild beasts at Ephesus', probably a figure of speech; Ignatius uses the same verb for his literal fate in Rome.
Ignatius retells Matthew's star in larger terms, without quoting Matthew.
'God's bread' has the words of John 6:33; Lake prints John 6 in the margin of 5:2. Likeness of language, not proof that Ignatius read John's Gospel.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what Christians in Syria and Asia believed early in the second century, the letter is of the first importance: Polycarp, Irenaeus and Eusebius know Ignatius's letters, the short recension is the form that W. R. Schoedel (1987) and C. Munier (1993) describe as the scholarly consensus, though some twentieth-century scholars have challenged it (see the authorship section), and the letter shows a church with one overseer, elders and deacons, a common meal called 'the thanksgiving', and a sharp confession that Christ is God and truly human. The text is fair but not perfect: the Greek rests on one manuscript, and several lines (6:2; 9:1-2; 20:2) are disputed or corrupt. Its few historical statements fit Eusebius and Polycarp. Its teaching follows the New Testament closely on Christ and goes beyond it on church order.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to early Christian faith and life
sections.b: Very high. Ignatius writes within a lifetime of the apostles, in a letter whose setting other early writers confirm (Polycarp to the Philippians 9:1; 13:2; Eusebius 3.36). He shows how Paul's letters were used (and language that sometimes comes close to John's), how a church was ordered, and what was believed about Christ. Lightfoot judged that even if forged, the short Greek 'can hardly have been made later than the middle of the second century' and 'its witness would still be highly valuable' (The Christian Ministry, page 49).

Good but thin. The short Greek survives in a single manuscript (G), and Lake corrects it from the Latin, the Armenian, the Syriac and the long recension. In this letter Lake's footnotes mark sixteen places where witnesses or editors differ, among them 'God in man' or 'God come in the flesh' (7:2) and a sentence Lake thinks 'not improbably corrupt' (20:2). Lake judges the text 'fairly accurate, though ... by no means so good as that of I. Clement'.

The letter makes few: Ignatius is a prisoner from Syria on the way to Rome (1:2; 21:2), at Smyrna with Polycarp (21:1), visited by named Ephesians (1:3-2:1). These fit Eusebius and Polycarp. The year is less certain: Eusebius's Chronicle gives AD 108, Jerome the eleventh year of Trajan, and Lake reports that critics are 'by no means unanimous'. The dissent over genuineness is old (Dallaeus in 1666, Cureton for the Syriac only), and it was renewed in the twentieth century: the authorship section gives the Catholic Encyclopedia's judgment of 1910, with its caveat, and the later challenges and replies.

Matches: Christ truly God and truly human, born of Mary of David's line by the Holy Spirit, truly suffering and risen (7:2; 18:2, with John 1:14, Romans 1:3-4, Luke 1:35, 1 John 4:2); prayer for outsiders and no revenge (10, with Matthew 5:44, Romans 12:17); faith shown by its fruit (14:2, with Matthew 12:33).

Goes beyond: the single overseer over a council of elders, and the strength of 'look at the overseer as at the Lord himself' (6:1), where the New Testament often uses 'overseer' and 'elder' of one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7). The Catholic Encyclopedia reads it as showing that 'the hierarchy of the Church was instituted by Christ'; Lightfoot read it as a development from the council of elders, which he credited to the influence of the last apostles; the cards at Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3 give each church's teaching. The star outshining the sun and moon (19:2) adds details Matthew does not give. 'The medicine of immortality' (20:2) is read by Catholic teaching as the Eucharist (Catechism 1405) and by memorial traditions as a figure.

Conflicts: none on the central teaching of Christ. Readers who hold that the New Testament knows only one office of elder-overseer see 6:1 and 3:2 as going beyond, not against, Scripture; the site does not rank these readings.

how_to_read.b: Ignatius is thanking a church that came to him in his chains. Read the warnings in the light of the praise around them (6:2; 8:1; 9:1): he is not scolding.
The great passages, 7:2 and 18:2-19:3, are close to hymns. Read them aloud, line by line, and notice the pairs and the paradoxes: born and unborn, silence and shout, hidden and shining.

how_to_read.h: As a witness, not as Scripture
how_to_read.b: No church treats the letter as Scripture. Use it to see how the New Testament was read in the next generation, and weigh its teaching on the overseer and the bread against the New Testament texts the notes point to, as the churches themselves do in different ways.
